title: Sphere-inside-a-cube near miss at Oceana

tellings.quote: the object almost hit the the pilot and it was this uh spear inside a cube
and that's when one of those weird cubinous sphere UAPs split the section.
tellings.difference: Puts it during the Roosevelt carrier training exercise with VFA-11 off the East Coast rather than at Oceana, and says the object split the section.
tellings.link_reason: Both describe the Graves-sourced incident in which a sphere-inside-a-cube UAP passed between, or nearly hit, a section of Navy F-18s in 2014-2015.

as_told.title: UAP splits a section of F-18s during the carrier training exercise
as_told.place_text: Off the US East Coast, VFA-11 from USS Theodore Roosevelt

tellings.quote: As soon as they cross that threshold, boom, object shoots down the left or the right wing of the lead aircraft. Uh came within about 50 ft of the cockpit, which is extremely close.
tellings.difference: Describes the object as a dark cube inside a clear sphere passing within about 50 ft of the cockpit at the working-area entry, and says a HAZREP was filed.
tellings.link_reason: Both tell of the near miss in which a cube-and-sphere object passed between a section of jets off Virginia Beach/Oceana, as Graves relates it.

as_told.title: Near-miss with a dark cube inside a clear sphere
as_told.place_text: Entry point of the working area off Virginia Beach

tellings.quote: When you hear stories like Ryan Graves, Navy pilot, talk about a sphere inside a cube or other kind of exotic, you know, looking objects that do have pointy edges

as_told.title: Host cites Ryan Graves' account of a sphere inside a cube

plain: Around 2014 or 2015, near Naval Air Station Oceana in Virginia, an object that looked like a dark cube inside a clear sphere shot past a pair of Navy jets as they entered their training area and came "within about 50 ft of the cockpit" of the lead jet, according to the Navy fighter pilot Ryan Graves, who relays what squadron mates told him and says a hazard report, the Navy's formal safety report, was filed. A retired Navy admiral named Tim Gallaudet retells it from Graves, placing it during a carrier training exercise off the East Coast and saying the object split the pair of jets, and Michels mentions the shape in passing. If true, it means unknown objects were flying close enough to Navy jets to be a collision danger.
